faq.a: Yes; if the rate is too fast, too slow, or if underlying myocardial disease causes poor output, the patient may need urgent treatment.
faq.q: Can a patient be in sinus rhythm and still be unstable?

faq.a: No; junctional rhythm or ventricular escape rhythm can also be regular. ECG is required for confirmation.
faq.q: Is a regular pulse always sinus rhythm?

faq.a: It is a physiologic variation of heart rate with respiration, common in children and young adults, and is benign.
faq.q: What is sinus arrhythmia and is it normal?

exam: A 45‑year‑old with rheumatic heart disease presents with a regular 78 bpm pulse; ECG shows P‑QRS relationship but PR interval 0.22 s. — Identify the rhythm, explain why it is not NSR, and state the next step.
During a ward round you note a patient’s pulse is 48 bpm, regular, and you have no ECG. — What bedside assessment confirms sinus bradycardia and what would you do if the patient is symptomatic?
A malaria patient develops sudden tachycardia of 130 bpm with regular rhythm. — Distinguish sinus tachycardia from supraventricular tachycardia and outline immediate management.
You see a monitor showing sinus rhythm at 90 bpm but the patient is pulseless. — Explain the pathophysiology and the emergency actions required.
In a low‑resource clinic you cannot obtain an ECG; a patient complains of palpitations. — How would you use pulse examination to differentiate NSR from atrial fibrillation?
A patient on digoxin presents with a regular pulse of 55 bpm and mild nausea. — Discuss how digoxin toxicity can affect sinus rhythm and the key investigations.
Explain why maintaining sinus rhythm is particularly important in a patient with left‑ventricular dysfunction due to sickle‑cell cardiomyopathy.
A young adult shows a regular pulse that varies with breathing. — Name this finding, its mechanism, and whether it requires treatment.
ai.title: Normal Sinus Rhythm
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Normal sinus rhythm (NSR) is the heart's regular electrical pattern originating from the sino‑atrial node. Recognising NSR and its variations is essential for distinguishing benign findings from arrhythmias in low‑resource settings.

b: P wave before every QRS
PR interval 0.12–0.20 s
Rate 60–100 bpm
Regular rhythm (R‑R intervals equal)
sections.p: NSR is a regular rhythm where each P wave is followed by a QRS complex, the PR interval is <0.20 s, and the rate is 60–100 bpm. In young patients sinus arrhythmia (rate varies with respiration) is normal.

b: Intact SA node
Normal atrial conduction
No high‑grade AV block
Absence of electrolyte or drug‑induced disturbances
sections.p: NSR is the default rhythm when the SA node functions normally and no overriding ectopic focus or conduction block exists.

b: Regular pulse
Rate 60–100 bpm
No palpitations, dizziness or syncope
sections.p: Patients are usually asymptomatic. On bedside examination the pulse is regular, with a normal volume and rate. In low‑resource wards the rhythm is confirmed on a basic ECG or a portable monitor.

t.b: Is the rhythm sinus? – Confirms NSR or identifies abnormal P‑QRS relationship.
Is the pulse regular? – Supports ECG findings when ECG unavailable.
Are potassium, magnesium, calcium normal? – Abnormalities can convert NSR to ectopic rhythms; treat if abnormal.

b: Sudden change to irregular or very slow/fast rate
Loss of pulse despite ECG activity
Associated chest pain, dyspnoea, syncope
sections.p: NSR itself is not dangerous, but a sudden loss of NSR (e.g., pulseless electrical activity) signals cardiac arrest. In low‑resource settings, missed brady‑ or tachy‑arrhythmias can lead to hypotension, heart failure, or stroke.

b: Correct electrolyte disturbances (e.g., give potassium if <3.5 mmol/L)
Avoid excessive β‑blockers or calcium‑channel blockers in brady‑cardic patients
Treat underlying infection (malaria, TB, HIV‑related myocarditis) that may precipitate arrhythmia
If NSR lost, consider temporary pacing if brady‑cardia <40 bpm with symptoms
sections.p: Maintain NSR by treating reversible causes and avoiding drugs that depress SA‑node function. In patients with LV dysfunction, NSR is preferred over atrial‑fibrillation because it preserves atrial contribution to ventricular filling.

b: Check pulse at each ward round
Repeat ECG if symptoms develop
Educate patients to report palpitations or syncope
sections.p: Routine monitoring of pulse and periodic ECG (or bedside monitor) in patients with cardiac risk factors (e.g., rheumatic heart disease, sickle‑cell cardiomyopathy) helps detect early rhythm change.

b: Sinus tachycardia – rate >100 bpm, still regular with P‑QRS relationship
Sinus bradycardia – rate <60 bpm, regular with P‑QRS relationship
Atrial fibrillation – irregularly irregular, absent discrete P waves
sections.p: Sinus tachycardia, sinus bradycardia, and atrial fibrillation can look similar on a quick glance but differ in rate, regularity, and P‑wave morphology.

b: Cold‑induced sinus slowing may be misread as sinus bradycardia
Digitalis toxicity can produce atrial premature beats that mimic sinus rhythm
sections.p: In severe hypothermia or drug overdose, the ECG may show a regular rhythm with P waves but the underlying conduction is impaired; clinical correlation is essential.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden loss of pulse despite ECG activity
New onset chest pain, severe dyspnoea, or syncope
Rapid change from NSR to irregular or extreme tachy‑/brady‑cardia
